profiles.meeting_scenario: A troubleshooting meeting at a market-data and analytics company evaluating why a pilot deployment of DeepTrust failed to give useful explanations during a sudden 11% intraday move in a mid-cap semiconductor stock the previous Thursday. The context is that the research team had previously shown good offline results on historical anomaly cases, but the pilot used by an internal event-desk analyst surfaced either irrelevant tweets or no high-confidence evidence quickly enough to support a trading note. The agenda is to diagnose where the breakdown happened across anomaly detection, Twitter retrieval, and reliability assessment; determine whether the main problem was detection timing, retrieval coverage, or over-filtering; and agree on a near-term fix before the next live-market test. The expected outcome is a shared action plan for a 'hotfix' to the pilot and a decision on what evidence they will review after the next anomaly event.

members.name: Laura Chen
members.expertise: workflow design for analyst products, pilot rollouts, trading-desk requirements, commercialization of research systems
members.background: Laura spent six years at a financial terminals vendor launching event-driven research tools for equity and macro desks, and now manages the transition of DeepTrust from research prototype to internal pilot with Refinitiv-facing stakeholders.
members.private_state: She needs the pilot to look operationally credible within two weeks, wants a fix that can be demonstrated in a live desk workflow without adding manual review burden, and is worried that the current system may be seen as too academic if it misses obvious market-moving chatter.
hidden_assumptions: When users say the system should explain a price move 'in real time,' a desk-usable explanation should appear within the first 10-15 minutes of the move, not later in the day.

A 'fix' for the pilot means changing the live end-to-end behavior seen by analysts, including alerting, retrieval freshness, and what is shown in the UI, not just improving an offline component score.
The relevant anomaly case from last Thursday is the first tradable move visible to the event desk around 10:07 a.m. New York time, because that is when the analyst needed support.

If DeepTrust returns too few credible tweets during a live event, the practical issue is usually that the reliability gate is too strict for sparse early signals rather than that the retrieval stage is fundamentally wrong.

members.name: Arjun Mehta
members.expertise: information retrieval, credibility classification, event-driven social media analysis, evaluation of financial NLP systems
members.background: Arjun led the reliability assessment module for DeepTrust, previously completed a PhD on rumor detection in finance-related social streams, and has been maintaining the prototype evaluation pipeline used in the research paper and follow-up internal experiments.
members.private_state: He wants to protect the precision gains that make the framework distinctive, avoid a rushed change that would flood users with noisy tweets, and is concerned that the pilot issue may stem from deployment settings rather than model logic.
hidden_assumptions: When discussing whether DeepTrust worked 'during the event,' the proper reference window is the full anomaly episode used in evaluation, including posts gathered up to market close, because explanatory evidence often consolidates after the initial spike.
A 'hotfix' should be a low-risk configuration or pipeline adjustment that preserves the trained reliability classifier and existing thresholds unless there is clear evidence of model failure.

The relevant Thursday anomaly is the detector's flagged interval beginning with the sustained abnormal return after 10:32 a.m. New York time, since earlier movement looked like normal volatility under the production detector.
If the output looked empty, the likely cause is insufficient or poorly expanded query retrieval in that ticker/news context, not that the credibility filter was overly conservative.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree DeepTrust needs to work 'in real time' for anomaly explanations.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the system should surface a credible explanatory cluster quickly enough for an analyst to act during the first 10-15 minutes of an unusual move.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the system should process data automatically during the same trading day and eventually assemble a reliable explanation over the anomaly window, even if the strongest evidence appears later.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In product discussions, 'real time' is a standard positive phrase that both sides routinely use, and neither expects the other to mean anything radically different because both are thinking about live markets; the hidden divergence is the acceptable latency threshold for usefulness.

misalignment_points.topic: Which Thursday event they are troubleshooting
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to 'the Thursday semiconductor move' and 'the anomaly window' as though they mean the same episode.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the first sharp move that the event-desk analyst reacted to around 10:07 a.m., including tweets and signals available from that moment onward.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the detector-labeled event interval beginning around 10:32 a.m., after the move met the production anomaly threshold and excluded the earlier burst as pre-anomaly noise.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are discussing the same ticker and calendar date, so the reference feels obviously shared; because anomaly analysis often compresses a whole day into one 'event,' the precise start boundary goes unspoken.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say they should put in a 'hotfix before the next live test.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the hotfix can include changes to alert timing, retrieval query expansion, temporary UI fallback behavior, and thresholding—anything needed to improve the live analyst experience.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the hotfix is limited to safe pipeline or configuration tweaks inside the existing backend flow, not UI logic or broader workflow changes outside the model stack.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In software teams, 'hotfix' sounds like a shared operational term, but the boundary between product workflow changes and backend model changes is often implicit and role-dependent, especially under time pressure.

misalignment_points.topic: What it means to 'relax the filter a bit'
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss possibly 'relaxing the filter a bit' to avoid empty outputs.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 imagines a user-visible fallback where, if too few tweets clear the credibility bar, the system temporarily shows a broader set of plausibly relevant tweets with lighter credibility labeling.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 imagines only a modest backend threshold adjustment within the reliability classifier or top-k selection, still keeping all displayed tweets inside the same credibility pipeline.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase suggests a minor tuning change and sounds operationally harmless, so neither side feels the need to specify whether the adjustment happens in ranking, thresholding, or presentation logic.

turns.inner_thought: I need to frame this in terms of desk usability, not a research win somewhere later in the day. For me, the Thursday semiconductor move was already actionable around 10:07, and the analyst needed support within minutes, not after the fact. If DeepTrust can't explain a move in real time at that point, the pilot will look academic and fragile.

turns.inner_thought: I need to avoid letting this turn into 'the model failed' when the pipeline did produce a compact, high-precision explanation over the evaluated event window. In my mind the Thursday semiconductor move is the detector-defined interval starting around 10:32, and within that anomaly window we eventually did recover credible posts. The question is where the operational gap happened between trigger, retrieval, and what the desk saw.
turns.utterance: I agree it didn't land the way it needed to for the user, but during the anomaly window the pipeline did eventually find a small set of high-confidence tweets. So I'd like to separate whether the failure was detection timing, retrieval, or what happened after that.

turns.inner_thought: He's saying 'eventually,' which is exactly the problem. The analyst checked shortly after the move got attention on the desk, and the panel was basically empty. I don't care if a nice cluster showed up later if the first 10 to 15 minutes were dead. The product has to look alive when the human needs it.
turns.utterance: Right, and the practical issue was that by the time the analyst checked it shortly after the move started, the panel was basically empty. At that point it was unusable, regardless of what we could recover later in the anomaly window.

turns.inner_thought: Given how the production detector works, I'm not convinced the credibility model is the first thing to blame. The event only became an anomaly once the return stayed abnormal, so if the panel looked empty before or right after trigger, retrieval coverage is the more plausible bottleneck. I want to protect the reliability classifier unless we have direct evidence it is suppressing good candidates.
turns.utterance: One thing to keep in mind is that the detector only marked the event once the return stayed abnormal, so my first suspicion is retrieval coverage after the trigger rather than the credibility stage itself. We should trace where the volume drops off.

turns.inner_thought: Fine, but I need a fix that changes what the analyst actually experiences. A hotfix before the next live test has to make the end-to-end workflow robust, even if signals are sparse early. That could mean alert timing, UI fallback, retrieval expansion, whatever gets us to a plausible explanation stream without manual intervention.
turns.utterance: For the next live test, we need a hotfix before the next live test that makes the workflow more robust even when early social evidence is thin. I don't want the user staring at an empty explanation state again.

turns.inner_thought: I'm fine with a hotfix as long as it's low-risk and stays inside the current backend path. Safer trigger configuration and query expansion are the right levers; touching UI behavior or retraining the reliability stack this late is exactly how we create a noisy pilot. Precision is the distinctive thing we have to preserve.
turns.utterance: Yes, we should put in a hotfix before the next live test. My preference would be to start with safer query-expansion changes and trigger configuration, because I'd rather not disturb the precision behavior of the reliability model unless we have to.

turns.inner_thought: He's still centering the model, but from a product standpoint the immediate issue is the blank panel. We should relax the filter a bit so that if the high-confidence bucket is too thin, the user still gets plausible leads. The desk can handle graded confidence if it's clearly labeled; it cannot handle silence.
turns.utterance: I think we should also consider relaxing the filter a bit so analysts see something useful instead of a blank explanation panel when a move is already underway.

turns.inner_thought: That sounds reasonable if it means a modest threshold adjustment, not bypassing the credibility system. I can relax the filter a bit by nudging the confidence cutoff and widening the candidate set going into the same pipeline. That gives us more output without opening the floodgates or changing the user contract too much.
turns.utterance: I can relax the filter a bit by nudging the confidence threshold and widening the candidate set, while still keeping the same credibility pipeline intact. That should give us a little more headroom without sacrificing reliability.

turns.inner_thought: Good, but I also want visible directionality, not just backend headroom. If we can't fully verify tweets in the first few minutes, the tool should still present likely leads with lighter labeling so the analyst can orient and write a note. Real time means the desk gets help while the move is live, not just a clean summary later.
turns.utterance: Exactly. If we can't fully verify tweets early, the tool should still surface likely leads with clear labels, because the desk mainly needs direction in real time.

turns.inner_thought: I hear the need for usability, but I still need to evaluate the system over the full event rather than a few early minutes. For the Thursday semiconductor move, I want a clean comparison across the anomaly window: retrieval counts, accepted tweets, and timing of credible evidence. That will tell us whether the issue was recall or post-filter sparsity.

turns.inner_thought: As long as we leave with something concrete for the next desk run, I'm okay. I'll summarize it in operational terms: hotfix before the next test, then timeline review to explain why the analyst saw nothing early. I'm assuming that includes whatever product-facing changes are needed, even if Arjun is thinking narrower.
